units.translation: b. ἐνωπαδίς: from behind, from opposite. Lᴳ P
725-26. ἵετο δ’ αὖ κούρης: she was eager to hear her voice, reasoning that she is descended from Helios, from the brightness of her eyes.
728-29 a. ἐπεὶ βλεφάρων ἀποτηλόθι: since they shone very far from the eyes with their rays.
b. They sent forth a golden ray opposite. Lᵐ (P)
734-36. Medea fabricated a story, saying that she had fled for this reason, because she feared her father, since she had helped Jason out of pity for her sister Chalciope.
746. ἄιστον: invisible, unknown. Lᴳ Sᴹ P
747. ἐφέστιος: being at my house. Lᴳ (P)

761-65 a. ὅθι τ’ ἄκμονες Ἡφαίστοιο: the islands of Aeolus are seven. On the one called Lipara or Strongyle, Hephaestus is thought to spend his time, and the roar of fire and the sound of hammers are heard.

In ancient times it was said that anyone who wished could bring unwrought iron and on the next day receive either a sword or whatever else he wanted to have made, and he would pay the wage. Pytheas records these things in his Circuit of the Earth (fg 4 A. Schmekel Progr. gymn. Merseb. 1848, 13), also saying that the sea boils. The islands of Aeolus are these seven: Strongyle, Euonymus, Lipara, Hiera, Didyme, Ericodes, Phoenicodes.

b. ἐλθεῖν εἰς ἀκτάς: Agathocles in his Commentaries (fg 9 M. IV 290), speaking about the forges of Hephaestus, says that there are two islands near Sicily, of which one is called Hiera and the other Strongyle, which emit fire day and night. The same author says that there are seven islands in Sicily; of these two emit fire, and one is called Aeolus' island, the other Hephaestus'; on the latter rivers of fire rise up.

d. αἰθρηγενέεσσιν ἀνά〈σσει〉: to those who produce clear sky and cold. That Aeolus had power over the winds, Homer also says (κ 21): 'For the son of Cronus made him keeper of the winds.' That they call cold 'αἴθρα', the same poet says (Ξ 318): 'overcome by clear sky and toil'. And we in common speech call things blown by the wind 'ὑπαίθρια'.
786-87. The Wandering Rocks are in the strait, as Timaeus (fg 5 M. I 194) and Peisistratus of Lipara (fg 1 M. IV 478) say. It must be read with hyperbaton: for it is 'διὰ περώντας'.
788. περιβλύει: washes around, in imitation of the sound. 'σπιλάδες' are rocks, from being compacted.
807. φιτύσαιο: may you plant or cause to grow. Lᴳ (P)
808-09. αὐτὴ δὲ σέλας χ〈είρεσσιν〉: that in ancient times the

mothers of the bridegrooms had the custom of carrying torches at weddings, and Euripides in the Phoenician Women says (344-46): 'But I did not kindle for you the lawful light of fire, as is fitting for a blessed mother.' Hera therefore says that she carried the torch for Thetis, performing the office of a mother because of her goodwill toward her.
